individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces V^3, a continuous spatio-temporal video super-resolution method built on a Video Fourier Field (VFF): a finite sum of 3D sinusoidal basis functions parameterized per local voxel by predicted amplitudes and phases. A neural encoder (RVRT) maps the low-resolution input to coefficient grids; a Gaussian PSF-aware sampler rescales basis functions in closed form for anti-aliasing. The method supports arbitrary spatial and temporal upsampling without explicit warping in the representation, and is evaluated on C-STVSR benchmarks (Adobe240, GoPro, Vid4) and special cases (AVSR, VFI), reporting sizable PSNR/SSIM improvements over prior art and reduced inference time.
Strengths: The unified 3D Fourier field is a conceptually simple and interpretable continuous representation that naturally supports arbitrary spatial and temporal sampling and avoids error-prone feature warping in the sampler.
Closed-form Gaussian PSF anti-aliasing (Eq. 4) is elegant, parameter-efficient, and theoretically motivated, addressing a real limitation of INR-based C-STVSR methods.

Strong empirical results: V^3 outperforms prior C-STVSR baselines by >1.5 dB PSNR on multiple benchmarks, sets a new state of the art on center and average frames, and improves temporal consistency (tOF).
The paper includes useful decoupling experiments (spatial-only and temporal-only SR) and a visual temporal-consistency analysis, demonstrating the generality of the representation.
The method is computationally efficient (1.27 s inference vs 1.88-1.90 s for MoTIF/BF-STVSR; lower VRAM than those methods).
Weaknesses: The comparison is not controlled: V^3 uses a strong RVRT backbone with RAFT optical flow and guided deformable attention, while baselines use different backbones; without an ablation replacing VFF with an INR/flow-warpping head on the same backbone, the reported gains cannot be attributed solely to the Fourier representation.

Several implementation details needed for reproduction are missing: the training loss (e.g., L1 vs L2) is not stated; frequency initialization/range, voxel size, coordinate normalization, and the architecture of the coefficient prediction head are not described.
Continuity across local voxel boundaries is not addressed; if amplitudes/phases change abruptly between voxels, sampling near boundaries may introduce discontinuities or artifacts.

The Gaussian PSF formula in Eq. (4) appears inconsistent with standard Fourier convolution conventions (e.g., for angular frequency the attenuation factor should be exp(-σ^2||ω||^2/2), not exp(-||ω||^2/(8π^2σ^2))), and the extension to per-dimension σ is not shown.
The claim of avoiding explicit warping is overstated because the RVRT encoder relies on RAFT flow and guided deformable attention; the method still depends on optical flow internally.

No statistical significance or multiple-run results are reported, and the benefits of the PSF-aware sampling are not demonstrated by a dedicated ablation (e.g., with/without anti-aliasing at out-of-distribution scales).
Questions: What is the exact training loss (L1, L2, or a combination) and how are the ground-truth coordinates sampled?
How are VFF parameters handled for query points at voxel boundaries: are amplitudes and phases trilinearly interpolated, and is the resulting field continuous?
Can you provide an ablation with the same RVRT backbone but with an INR/warping-based head (or with a flow-free backbone) to isolate the contribution of the VFF representation?
What is the precise definition of σ in Eq. (4) and how does the formula relate to the standard Gaussian convolution theorem for angular frequencies? How are per-dimension σ values applied?
How are the 512 frequencies initialized and constrained during training? Is there any frequency selection or learnable bandwidth per voxel?
Does V^3 require any post-processing or boundary blending when sampling across voxels in a large output grid?
Does the RAFT component in RVRT remain fixed for most training; if so, how much do the flow-based features contribute to the final performance?
Limitations: The finite Fourier basis may over-smooth very high-frequency content at high upscaling factors, and the paper only acknowledges this qualitatively without quantifying the trade-off.
The method is not evaluated under realistic degradations (noise, motion blur, compression artifacts); the extension to such degradations is only discussed in future work.
No analysis of failure cases, such as videos with large occlusions, complex non-periodic motion, or long-term drift.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts (e.g., deepfake generation or surveillance enhancement) or provide broader-impact considerations.
The reported runtime is measured on a fixed patch size and may not reflect full-video inference; memory/throughput at larger resolutions is not analyzed.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper introduces V^3, a continuous space-time video super-resolution (C-STVSR) method built on a novel Video Fourier Field (VFF) representation. Rather than separating spatial and temporal modeling and relying on explicit optical-flow warping, VFF represents video as a finite sum of 3D sinusoidal basis functions over local voxels, with coefficients predicted by a video backbone encoder. This unified representation supports arbitrary spatial and temporal upsampling, closed-form anti-aliasing with a Gaussian point spread function, and longer temporal context. Experiments on Vid4, GoPro, Adobe240, and REDS show substantial PSNR/SSIM improvements over prior C-STVSR methods (VideoINR, MoTIF, BF-STVSR) and dedicated AVSR methods, along with improved temporal consistency and lower inference time.
Strengths: Proposes a conceptually novel unified spatio-temporal frequency representation that avoids explicit flow-based warping in the output representation, naturally supporting arbitrary space-time sampling.
Provides a principled and efficient anti-aliasing mechanism through an analytic Gaussian PSF, which is exact for the Fourier basis and avoids learned filtering used by prior methods.

Reports large empirical gains: >1.5 dB PSNR over BF-STVSR on Adobe/GoPro C-STVSR, and >1 dB over dedicated AVSR methods when trained for AVSR, with consistent improvements in temporal consistency (tOF).
Shows computational advantages: faster inference than VideoINR, MoTIF, and BF-STVSR on the measured setting, while using competitive memory.
Ablates the unified representation by evaluating spatial-only and temporal-only SR, demonstrating that the same model excels in both edge cases.
Clear writing and well-organized presentation with informative qualitative comparisons and quantitative tables.
Weaknesses: Critical implementation details are omitted: voxel grid geometry (size, overlap), boundary handling between voxels, how the N=512 frequencies are initialized/learned, how the conv head maps features to amplitudes/phases, and how the Gaussian PSF sigma is selected for each sampling scale.

The finite Fourier basis with a shared frequency set may be a representational bottleneck for non-translational motion, complex occlusions, or very high-frequency textures; no analysis of capacity or failure cases is provided.

Although the VFF avoids explicit warping, the backbone encoder (RVRT) still internally uses RAFT optical flow, so the end-to-end system is not completely independent of flow estimation, which weakens the paper's motivation.
Evaluation is limited to synthetic bicubic degradation and temporal subsampling; no experiments with realistic degradations (noise, motion blur, compression) despite the method's claimed generality.

Baseline comparisons may be partly unfair because V^3 uses a modern, strong backbone (RVRT) with 13.7M parameters, while some baselines use weaker encoders; the paper does not control for backbone capacity or provide compute-matched comparisons.
No perceptual metrics (LPIPS, DISTS, user study) or generative baselines are included, so the claim of 'sharper' results relies primarily on PSNR/SSIM and qualitative examples.
The method is trained only on Adobe240 for C-STVSR, and generalization to diverse real-world videos is underexplored.
Questions: How are the local voxel regions defined? What are their sizes, overlap, and how is continuity across voxel boundaries enforced?
How are the N=512 frequencies chosen or learned? Are they sampled from a distribution, optimized jointly, or fixed after pretraining?
How is the Gaussian PSF sigma determined for different spatial/temporal scale factors, and is it tuned per dataset or per degradation?
What is the effect of varying the number of basis functions N, voxel resolution, or the shared frequency set on quality and compute?
Does the method handle non-translational motion, large occlusions, or periodic textures, and are there failure cases where the Fourier basis is insufficient?
How does V^3 perform under realistic degradations (e.g., blur, noise, compression) or out-of-distribution scaling factors beyond x8?
Since the RVRT backbone includes RAFT flow, what is the contribution of the flow component versus the VFF representation to the final performance?
Limitations: Discriminative training with a regression objective tends to produce over-smoothed outputs at high scaling factors; no perceptual/generative objective is considered.
The finite Fourier basis and local voxelization may introduce representational limitations or boundary artifacts, especially for very high frequencies.
Training is computationally heavy: 2.5 million iterations on 16 GH200 GPUs, which may limit reproducibility and accessibility.
Evaluation is restricted to synthetic degradations (bicubic downsampling + temporal subsampling), so real-world applicability is not demonstrated.
The method still relies on an optical-flow-based backbone (RVRT/RAFT) for feature aggregation, which may carry some of the same errors the representation aims to avoid.
Potential negative societal impacts of improved video super-resolution (e.g., deepfakes, surveillance) are not discussed, though this is not a major concern for the paper.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes V^3, a continuous spatio-temporal video super-resolution method based on a Video Fourier Field (VFF), which represents video as a finite sum of 3D sinusoidal basis functions in (x,y,t). The coefficients are predicted by a neural video encoder with a large spatio-temporal receptive field, and the representation can be sampled at arbitrary spatial and temporal resolutions. A closed-form Gaussian PSF factor is introduced for anti-aliasing. The method is evaluated on C-STVSR, arbitrary-scale video SR, and video frame interpolation, showing consistent PSNR/SSIM improvements over prior methods while being computationally efficient.
Strengths: The VFF representation is conceptually simple and novel: a single joint spatio-temporal trigonometric expansion avoids the explicit warping used by prior C-STVSR methods for output reconstruction.
The closed-form PSF-aware sampling (Eq. 4) is parameter-efficient and offers a principled way to handle anti-aliasing at arbitrary scales, a capability that prior methods lack.

Extensive experiments show large and consistent improvements (up to ~2 dB PSNR) across multiple benchmarks, including the edge cases of spatial-only and temporal-only SR, with better temporal consistency.
The method is computationally efficient: inference is faster than all compared continuous STVSR baselines and uses moderate memory, making it practical.
The paper is generally well-written and clearly explains the limitations of prior warping-based approaches and the advantages of a unified spatio-temporal representation.
Weaknesses: The Gaussian PSF anti-aliasing factor in Eq. 4 appears questionable: for a Gaussian PSF with variance sigma, the attenuation should increase with sigma, but exp(-||omega||^2/(8*pi^2*sigma^2)) gives less attenuation for larger sigma. This is likely a typo, but as written it undermines the anti-aliasing claim and needs clarification/correction.

The claim of avoiding explicit warping is overstated because the backbone encoder RVRT includes a finetuned RAFT optical-flow component (mentioned in Sec. 3.4). The 'warping-free' property applies only to the output representation, not to the feature encoder, and this should be acknowledged.

Key implementation details are missing: the exact local voxel grid tiling, how the shared frequencies are initialized/selected, the loss function used for training, and how the temporal PSF/sigma is set during training and inference are not specified, making reproduction difficult.

Quantitative evaluation lacks error bars, statistical significance tests, and is limited to PSNR/SSIM; no perceptual quality metric or user study is reported, which is important for super-resolution tasks.

The VFF is a finite, non-orthogonal sum of fixed sinusoids; no analysis is provided of its representational capacity for very complex motions, large displacements, or potential seam artifacts at voxel boundaries.

Comparisons in Table 2 mix methods trained on different datasets/domains (e.g., arbitrary-scale image SR models versus the proposed model trained on Adobe240), making the comparison less direct than claimed.
Questions: Can the authors provide a derivation of Eq. 4? For a Gaussian PSF with variance sigma, the Fourier transform should scale as exp(-sigma^2 ||omega||^2 / 2), not exp(-||omega||^2/(8 pi^2 sigma^2)). Please clarify the exact definition of sigma and why the exponent is inverted.

How exactly are local voxels defined (size, overlap, number of voxels per input frame)? How are the shared frequencies {omega_i} initialized and selected during training? What happens at voxel boundaries to ensure continuity?
What loss function is used for training (e.g., L1, Charbonnier, perceptual)? Is temporal consistency enforced explicitly during training, or only indirectly through the representation?

Since the backbone RVRT includes a finetuned RAFT optical-flow component, what role does optical flow play in feature aggregation, and how does this align with the paper's emphasis on avoiding warping?
Are the reported PSNR/SSIM numbers averaged over multiple runs? Were the differences statistically tested against the closest baselines?
How is the temporal PSF/sigma_t chosen for temporal upsampling? Is it set to a fixed value or learned? Does anti-aliasing in time behave differently from space, given that frame subsampling is used?
Limitations: The as-written anti-aliasing formula appears technically incorrect, which, if uncorrected, calls into question the central advantage of principled aliasing-free sampling.
The method still relies on an optical-flow component within the encoder, inheriting potential flow errors that the paper claims to avoid.
The paper lacks sufficient implementation details for replication, including loss function, voxel grid, frequency basis initialization, and PSF parameter settings.

Evaluation is limited to synthetic bicubic downsampling and subsampled frames; real-world degradations (noise, motion blur, compression) are not addressed despite the PSF framework being capable of doing so.
As acknowledged by the authors, the method tends to produce over-smoothed results at very high scaling factors due to discriminative training; no perceptual or generative refinement is considered.
The VFF representation may become a bottleneck for long-term temporal dynamics or very large scenes, and the fixed shared-frequency basis could limit adaptability to different content.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces V^3, a continuous space-time video super-resolution method. It proposes a Video Fourier Field (VFF): videos are represented as a finite sum of 3D sinusoidal basis functions over local voxels, whose amplitudes and phases are predicted by a neural video encoder from a low-resolution input. Sampling can be done at arbitrary spatial/temporal resolutions, and a closed-form Gaussian PSF factor is used for anti-aliasing. Experiments on C-STVSR benchmarks show substantial PSNR/SSIM improvements over prior INR/warping-based methods, as well as improved temporal consistency and lower inference time.
Strengths: A unified 3D Fourier representation jointly models space and time, avoiding explicit optical-flow warping and enabling multi-frame context; this is conceptually simple and interpretable.
The closed-form Gaussian PSF sampling for anti-aliasing is principled and computationally efficient, a nice alternative to learned PSF.
Strong empirical results: ~2 dB PSNR gains over prior C-STVSR methods across Adobe240, GoPro, Vid4, and REDS; also demonstrates better temporal consistency and lower runtime.
The paper includes several complementary evaluations (C-STVSR, AVSR, VFI, temporal consistency, complexity) and ablates model size.
Weaknesses: The technical description is incomplete: Eq. (3) defines a scalar field, but the target is an RGB video; it is not explained how the three color channels are generated. Voxel tiling, frequency initialization, coordinate normalization, and boundary continuity are also underspecified.

The anti-aliasing claim may not match the actual degradation: LR inputs are created by bicubic downsampling, while the sampler assumes a Gaussian PSF; no evidence is given that this PSF matches the training data distribution.
No ablations are provided for key design choices (N, voxel size, shared frequencies, PSF, encoder backbone), so the source of the gains is unclear.

Comparisons may be unfair: Table 2 compares C-STVSR models trained on Adobe240 against image AISR methods trained on other data, and Table 5 includes a model (ST-AVSR) with an auxiliary pretrained VGG-16; no error bars or statistical significance are reported.
Some claims are overstated, e.g., first continuous method to surpass per-frame AISR, without controlling training-domain shifts.
Questions: How does the scalar VFF in Eq. (3) produce three color channels? Are there separate coefficient sets per channel or vector-valued amplitudes?
What are the exact basis frequencies and voxelization parameters (voxel size, overlap, coordinate normalization)? How is continuity across voxel boundaries guaranteed?
Is the Gaussian PSF used during training? How is its sigma chosen relative to the bicubic downsampling used to generate LR inputs?

review.Summary: The paper introduces VFF, a continuous video representation based on a finite sum of 3D sinusoidal basis functions over (x,y,t), and an end-to-end framework V^3 that predicts local amplitudes and phases from a low-resolution input video using a neural encoder. VFF permits arbitrary spatial and temporal sampling and supports closed-form Gaussian point-spread-function sampling for anti-aliasing. The method avoids explicit warping at the output stage and is evaluated for space-time super-resolution, spatial-only super-resolution, and video frame interpolation, reporting substantial PSNR/SSIM gains over prior C-STVSR baselines on Vid4, GoPro, Adobe240, and REDS, alongside faster inference.
Strengths: The VFF representation is conceptually simple and novel: a unified 3D Fourier-like field with shared frequencies and per-voxel amplitudes/phases enables continuous sampling in space and time without explicit frame warping at the output stage.
The closed-form Gaussian PSF sampling provides a principled and efficient anti-aliasing mechanism, unlike learned scale-adaptive filtering in prior C-STVSR methods.
The empirical results are strong: V^3 outperforms prior C-STVSR methods by roughly 1.5–2 dB PSNR across multiple benchmarks and tasks, and improves temporal consistency as measured by tOF.
The method is computationally efficient: inference is faster than competing C-STVSR models with moderate VRAM usage.
The paper is generally well-organized and includes clear figures and supplementary qualitative results.
Weaknesses: The paper omits key implementation details needed for reproduction: voxel boundary handling, frequency initialization and sharing, coordinate normalization, selection of sigma for each target scale, and the exact sampling procedure for arbitrary coordinates.

The claim of avoiding explicit warping is weakened because the RVRT backbone uses RAFT optical flow and deformable attention; the paper does not analyze how much of the gain comes from the VFF output representation versus the flow-based temporal aggregation in the encoder.

The anti-aliasing formulation is presented as exact, but the paper does not derive the PSF formula or discuss truncation effects at voxel boundaries, nor how sigma relates to the output sampling rate; without this, the anti-aliasing guarantee is not substantiated.

The evaluation is limited to PSNR/SSIM, with no perceptual metrics, statistical significance tests, or real-world degradations. Several baseline numbers appear copied from previous papers, and some table cells are missing, making comparisons difficult to verify.
The paper trains only on scale factors 1.2–4 but evaluates out-of-distribution scales 6 and 8 without explaining how the fixed frequency basis and PSF settings generalize.
Questions: How are voxel boundaries handled? Is the VFF continuous across neighboring cells, or are fields sampled independently per cell, potentially producing seams?
How are the N=512 frequencies initialized or selected, and are they learned jointly with the encoder? Are they normalized to voxel dimensions and temporal duration?
Since the backbone uses RAFT optical flow, how can the paper claim to avoid warping-based temporal modeling? What is the exact role of flow inside RVRT for predicting VFF parameters?

How is the Gaussian PSF variance sigma chosen for each desired output resolution? Is it fixed, learned, or derived from the sampling grid, and how does it affect in-distribution vs out-of-distribution scales?
What loss function is used (e.g., L1, L2, perceptual)? Is supervision applied at randomly sampled continuous coordinates or only on the output raster?
For long videos, how is the temporal context handled beyond the 14-frame training window? Are there overlapping chunks, and does the local VFF grid size always equal the input resolution?

Are the baseline results in Tables 1–4 recomputed with the authors' own evaluation pipeline or copied from the original papers? If copied, are the training settings and evaluation protocols identical?
Limitations: The discriminative training objective is acknowledged to cause oversmoothing at very high scaling factors; no perceptual or user-study evaluation is provided.
A finite Fourier basis may be a representational bottleneck for very high-frequency content or large, complex motions; no failure analysis is given.
Only bicubic spatial downsampling and uniform temporal subsampling are considered; real-world degradations such as noise, compression artifacts, and motion blur are not handled.
Training is computationally expensive (16 GH200 chips for 2.5M iterations), which may limit reproducibility and accessibility.
Possible negative societal impact: super-resolution can be misused to fabricate or manipulate video content; the paper does not discuss this.

review.Summary: The paper introduces V^3, a continuous spatio-temporal video super-resolution method based on a Video Fourier Field (VFF), which represents video as a finite sum of 3D sinusoidal basis functions over local voxels, with amplitudes and phases predicted by a neural video encoder. The representation supports arbitrary spatial and temporal sampling and includes a closed-form Gaussian point-spread-function factor for anti-aliasing. Experiments on C-STVSR benchmarks and edge cases such as arbitrary-scale video SR and video frame interpolation report substantial PSNR/SSIM gains over prior INR/warping-based methods, improved temporal consistency, and lower inference time.
Strengths: The VFF is a conceptually novel and unified 3D Fourier representation that naturally enables arbitrary space-time sampling and avoids explicit warping at the output stage.
The closed-form Gaussian PSF anti-aliasing is elegant, parameter-efficient, and theoretically motivated, though its exact formulation needs clarification.
Strong empirical results: large PSNR/SSIM improvements over prior C-STVSR baselines across multiple benchmarks, with better temporal consistency and faster inference.
The method is evaluated on multiple tasks (C-STVSR, AVSR, VFI), including spatial-only and temporal-only edge cases, demonstrating generality.
Useful decoupling experiments and computational comparisons are included.
Weaknesses: Key implementation details are missing: the exact training loss, voxel grid geometry, frequency initialization/selection, coordinate normalization, coefficient prediction head, and how RGB channels are generated from a scalar Fourier field.

The Gaussian PSF anti-aliasing formula in Eq. (4) appears inconsistent with standard Fourier convolution conventions as written, and no derivation or clarification of sigma is provided, undermining a central claim.
The claim of avoiding explicit warping is overstated because the RVRT backbone internally uses RAFT optical flow and guided deformable attention; only the output representation is warping-free.
Comparisons are not controlled: V^3 uses a stronger RVRT backbone, baselines may use different training data, and no ablation isolates the contribution of VFF from the backbone.
Evaluation is limited to PSNR/SSIM on synthetic bicubic degradation; no perceptual metrics, statistical significance tests, or real-world degradations are reported.
No analysis is provided for voxel-boundary continuity, potential seam artifacts, representational limitations for complex motion/occlusions, or failure cases.
Training is computationally heavy (2.5M iterations on 16 GH200 GPUs), and no code is released, limiting reproducibility.
Questions: How is Eq. (4) derived? For Gaussian PSF filtering, the attenuation should increase with sigma; the current formula appears to do the opposite. What is the exact definition of sigma and how is it set for different scales?
How exactly are local voxels defined (size, overlap, tiling), and what mechanism ensures continuity of the VFF across voxel boundaries?
How are the N=512 frequencies initialized, selected, or learned? Are they shared across voxels and normalized to voxel dimensions?
What training loss is used (L1, L2, Charbonnier, perceptual)? Is temporal consistency enforced explicitly?
How are RGB color channels generated from the scalar VFF in Eq. (3)?
What is the relative contribution of the VFF output representation versus the RAFT-flow-based RVRT encoder? Can an ablation replace VFF with an INR head on the same backbone?
How do the reported results change with error bars or multiple runs, and were baseline numbers recomputed under identical protocols?
Limitations: Discriminative regression training leads to oversmoothing at very high upscaling factors; no perceptual or generative refinement is considered.
The finite Fourier basis may limit high-frequency content and complex non-periodic motion, but this is not analyzed quantitatively.
Only synthetic bicubic downsampling and uniform temporal subsampling are evaluated; noise, motion blur, compression artifacts, and other real-world degradations are not.
Voxel-boundary artifacts and failures on large occlusions or long-term drift are not investigated.
Potential negative societal impacts of improved video super-resolution, such as deepfake generation or surveillance enhancement, are not discussed.
